meta.title: Six ideas for three weeks
meta.tagline: Drawn from the team's own work: a logistics company, four developers, about ten hours a week each. **Example content: replace every value.**

ideas.headline: Six directions, one recommendation
ideas.lead: Each idea names who it helps, the moment the demo turns on, and the reason it could fail. The scores are ours, against the four judging criteria.

items.title: Invoice exceptions, resolved before lunch
items.pitch: An agent reads a blocked supplier invoice, finds why it does not match the order, and hands the clerk a decision.
items.who: Four accounts payable clerks who lose three days per blocked invoice waiting for answers.
items.demo: A blocked invoice opens with the cause already named and the supplier's email quoted as proof.
items.why: The pain is measured, the data can be synthetic, and a person approves every release, so it is safe to show.
items.risk: The agent names the wrong cause; the approval step has to be visible in the demo.
items.verdict: Recommended: the only idea where the number that matters is already measured, and the demo is one screen.

items.title: The 2009 tariff engine, readable again
items.pitch: Bob maps a legacy rating module, writes the tests it never had, and moves one tariff family to a service.
items.who: Two developers who are the only people allowed to touch the tariff code.
items.demo: The same shipment priced by the old module and the new service, with the test suite green on both.
items.why: Modernisation is one of the four directions the challenge names, and the before and after are easy to prove.
items.risk: The value is real but invisible to a non-technical judge unless the demo shows a change shipped in minutes.

items.title: Ask the warehouse
items.pitch: An MCP server over the warehouse system, so Bob and any agent can answer stock questions in plain language.
items.who: Sales staff who phone the warehouse about thirty times a day.
items.demo: A salesperson asks where an order is and gets the shelf, the picker and the promised time.
items.why: It opens the company's own system to every later agent, which is the scaling story.
items.risk: Read-only access to the warehouse system must be granted in week one or the idea stalls.

items.title: Quote in a minute
items.pitch: A small web app that turns a customer's email into a priced quote, checked against capacity.
items.who: The sales desk, which answers a quote request in four hours on average.
items.demo: Paste a real request, get a quote with the route, the price and the reasoning.
items.why: Revenue is the easiest value to explain, and the app is a blank page Bob can fill fast.
items.risk: Pricing rules live in people's heads; the first week goes into writing them down.

items.title: Customs papers that check themselves
items.pitch: An agent compares a customs declaration with the commercial invoice and flags what a broker would reject.
items.who: Three customs coordinators and every customer whose cargo waits at the border.
items.demo: A declaration with two planted errors: the agent finds both and cites the rule.
items.why: The cost of one held container makes the business case in a single sentence.
items.risk: The rules differ by country; the slice must be one corridor only.

items.title: Driver onboarding without the binder
items.pitch: Replace the paper onboarding of contract drivers with a guided chat that collects documents and books the safety briefing.
items.who: The fleet office and about twenty new drivers a month.
items.demo: A driver finishes onboarding on a phone in the time it takes to drink a coffee.
items.why: Not an improvement of the old process: the binder and two of its five approvals disappear.
items.risk: Document checks touch personal data, so the proof of concept must run on invented drivers.
